name: Belle Isle Null
description:
Belle Isle was a public park for 150 years — 982 acres of green space in the Detroit River, accessible by a single bridge, home to an aquarium, a conservatory, and the kind of quiet that cities forget they need. When Cinderblock AI acquired sovereign rights to the island in 2167, the public access ended. The bridge was retrofit with biometric screening. The aquarium was emptied. The conservatory was sealed. And over the next three decades, every acre of the island was converted into what is now the largest edge computing installation in North America — the Cinderblock Detroit Neural Processing Array, commonly known as Belle Isle Null.

The island's geography was ideal: surrounded by river water for cooling, accessible by a single chokepoint for security, and far enough from residential areas that the electromagnetic output doesn't cause augment interference in the general population. The server farms are built low — single-story structures that follow the island's contours, connected by underground utility corridors and cooled by river water pumped through the foundations. From the air, the island looks like a circuit board laid over a park. The trees were kept. This was not environmental sensitivity — the tree canopy provides thermal regulation and visual screening from surveillance satellites. The deer that used to roam the park still roam the server corridors. Cinderblock's PR department calls them "the world's first AI-adjacent wildlife population." The maintenance technicians call them a navigation hazard.

Belle Isle Null processes 40% of the Detroit metro area's autonomous vehicle routing, all of Cinderblock AI's GLM neural network training operations, and — according to persistent rumors that Cinderblock has never dignified with a denial — the surveillance data integration for every corporate security force in the Detroit corridor. The island is a brain. Not metaphorically. Every autonomous vehicle decision, every facial recognition query, every predictive behavior model in the Detroit metro feeds through the processing arrays on this island. Whoever controls Belle Isle Null controls the nervous system of the city. Cinderblock knows this. Everyone else suspects it.

sights: Low server buildings following the island's natural contours, their surfaces camouflaged with living moss panels
The old tree canopy — oaks and elms maintained not for beauty but for thermal regulation and satellite screening
Deer walking between server building corridors, unconcerned by the hum of civilization's processing power
The single bridge approach — a chokepoint bristling with biometric, electromagnetic, and physical screening systems
Cooling water discharge points along the shore, where river water exits the server foundations warmer than it entered
sounds: The hum. The entire island hums — a frequency generated by processing power that would be silent in any single unit but becomes audible at this scale
Cooling water moving through underground channels — a constant liquid murmur beneath everything
Security drone patrols — more frequent and more aggressive than anywhere in the Detroit metro
Deer. Hooves on service paths, occasionally tripping proximity sensors and causing false security alerts that nobody finds funny anymore
Nothing human. The island's maintenance staff numbers 200, and they communicate by neural interface to avoid ambient noise contamination of the acoustic monitoring systems.
smells: Warm electronics and river water — the island's signature combination
Forest floor — the tree canopy still drops leaves, and the decomposition smell is incongruous with the technology beneath
Ozone from the processing arrays, strongest near the cooling discharge points
atmosphere.feel: Uncanny. Belle Isle Null feels like a place where nature and technology have reached an uneasy coexistence that neither chose. The trees are real. The deer are real. The park paths still exist. And beneath it all, a machine mind processes the data that makes the city function. Walking the island — if you could get access — would feel like walking on top of a sleeping giant's skull.

demographics: 200 maintenance technicians and 50 security personnel, working in rotating shifts. No permanent residents. The technicians are Tier 3, hand-selected by Cinderblock AI and subject to the most comprehensive background screening in the corporate sector. Average tenure: 14 years. Turnover is near zero because the security clearance makes leaving complicated.
economy: Cinderblock AI values the Belle Isle Null installation at Φ2.4 trillion. It generates no local commerce — the island is a closed system. Economic impact is measured in what it enables: the autonomous vehicle routing alone facilitates Φ12 billion in daily freight movement across the GLM.
power_structure: Cinderblock AI, absolutely and without exception. The island's director, Dr. Solomon Yates, reports directly to Cinderblock's global board. No other corporate or governmental authority has any jurisdiction. The island is sovereign Cinderblock territory under a 99-year charter that the State of Michigan signed in exchange for Φ45 billion in infrastructure funding.
dangers: Security response — unauthorized approach triggers lethal countermeasures with no warning protocol
Electromagnetic exposure — the processing array's output exceeds safe limits for unshielded neural interfaces in certain zones
Data vulnerability — if the island is compromised, every autonomous vehicle and surveillance system in the Detroit metro becomes unreliable
River current — the cooling water discharge creates treacherous currents around the island's perimeter
The deer — this is not a joke. A 180-pound white-tailed deer in a server corridor will damage equipment and personnel impartially.
opportunities: Data access — tapping into Belle Isle Null's processing stream would provide real-time intelligence on every corporate operation in the Detroit metro
AV routing manipulation — control the routing arrays and you control how every autonomous vehicle in the GLM moves
The 200 maintenance technicians know the island's physical layout, vulnerabilities, and security gaps — one cooperative technician is worth more than a hundred operatives
The cooling water discharge points are the island's physical weak spot — sabotage the cooling and the processing arrays overheat
story_hooks: A maintenance technician smuggles out a fragment of data from the processing arrays. The data shows that Belle Isle Null isn't just processing AV routing — it's running predictive models of individual citizens' behavior, and the accuracy exceeds what any known AI should achieve.

The island's deer population has been declining. Necropsies show neural tissue anomalies consistent with prolonged electromagnetic exposure. If the deer are affected, what about the 200 people who work there?

Someone is building a second, unauthorized processing layer beneath the existing installation. The power draw is visible in the utility logs but the physical infrastructure doesn't appear on any blueprint. Dr. Yates claims he doesn't know about it. His neural stress indicators suggest otherwise.
frequented_by: Nobody else — authorized access only, enforced lethally

notable_locations.name: The Processing Core
notable_locations.description: The central server cluster in the former picnic grounds — 200,000 square feet of edge computing power cooled by the Detroit River

notable_locations.name: The Bridge Checkpoint
notable_locations.description: The single access point — biometric, electromagnetic, and physical screening that takes eleven minutes and misses nothing

notable_locations.name: The Old Conservatory
notable_locations.description: Sealed since 2167, its glass dome still visible through the trees — rumored to house Dr. Yates' private research installation, but no maintenance technician has been inside in twenty years
